ch15_ex6_q1: You only need four numbers: every value in the table is $0$, $0.5$, $0.87$ or $1$ with a sign in front.
Shortcut: from $180^\circ$ to $360^\circ$ the values repeat those from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$ with the signs flipped, because $\sin(x + 180^\circ) = -\sin(x)$.
ch15_ex6_q2: Plot the five key points of each cycle first: $(0^\circ,0)$, $(90^\circ,1)$, $(180^\circ,0)$, $(270^\circ,-1)$, $(360^\circ,0)$. Then use the $30^\circ$ values to shape the curve between them.
With 1 cm $= 30^\circ$, the axis to $720^\circ$ is 24 cm long, so turn the graph paper landscape before you start.
ch15_ex6_q3: Unit circle reason: adding $360^\circ$ takes P once around the circle back to the same point, so every sine value repeats.
ch15_ex6_q4a: $42^\circ$ is close to $45^\circ$, and $\sin(45^\circ) \approx 0.71$, so a reading of about $0.7$ makes sense.
ch15_ex6_q4b: Use symmetry about $90^\circ$: $\sin(130^\circ) = \sin(50^\circ) \approx 0.77$, so read the easier rising part of the graph.
ch15_ex6_q4c: $\sin(160^\circ) = \sin(20^\circ)$, and the small-angle estimate $20 \times \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.35$ confirms a reading of about $0.3$.
ch15_ex6_q4d: $200^\circ$ is $20^\circ$ past $180^\circ$, so its value is the negative of the value $20^\circ$ after $0^\circ$: $-\sin(20^\circ) \approx -0.3$.
ch15_ex6_q5a: Sine crosses the axis at every multiple of $180^\circ$, so $0^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $360^\circ$, $540^\circ$ and $720^\circ$ all give exactly 0.
ch15_ex6_q5b: The wave is flat near its peak, so angles close to $90^\circ$ give values close to 1: $\sin(70^\circ) \approx 0.94$.
ch15_ex6_q5d: $290^\circ$ is $20^\circ$ past the minimum at $270^\circ$, so it mirrors $250^\circ$: both give about $-0.94$.
ch15_ex6_q6a: Calculator check: $\sin^{-1}(0.9) \approx 64.2^\circ$. Its partner in the same cycle is $180^\circ - 64^\circ = 116^\circ$; add $360^\circ$ to both for the second cycle.
ch15_ex6_q6b: For a negative sine value, use the positive reference angle $64^\circ$ and place it in quadrants 3 and 4: $180^\circ + 64^\circ = 244^\circ$ and $360^\circ - 64^\circ = 296^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q6c: $0.7$ is just under $\frac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707 = \sin(45^\circ)$, so the first answer must be just under $45^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q7a: $-0.5$ is an exact value: reference angle $30^\circ$, placed in quadrants 3 and 4, gives $210^\circ$ and $330^\circ$ with no estimating needed.
ch15_ex6_q7b: Link to the 3-4-5 triangle: $\sin^{-1}(0.8) \approx 53^\circ$, since $\sin = \frac45$ there. Then $180^\circ + 53^\circ = 233^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q7c: For sine, the two solutions in one cycle with positive $y$ always add to $180^\circ$: $24^\circ + 156^\circ = 180^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q8: Shortcut: $\cos(x) = \sin(x + 90^\circ)$, so the cosine row is the sine row read three columns ($90^\circ$) further along.
ch15_ex6_q9: Key points for one cycle: $(0^\circ,1)$, $(90^\circ,0)$, $(180^\circ,-1)$, $(270^\circ,0)$, $(360^\circ,1)$. The curve is symmetric about $x = 180^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q10: Unit circle reason: P just keeps going round the circle, so its $x$-coordinate keeps repeating the same pattern every $360^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q11: Check the $90^\circ$ shift with a value: $\sin(30^\circ + 90^\circ) = \sin(120^\circ) \approx 0.87 = \cos(30^\circ)$.
ch15_ex6_q12a: Values link across graphs: $\cos(48^\circ) = \sin(42^\circ) \approx 0.67$, since the angles add to $90^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q12b: $\cos(155^\circ) = -\cos(25^\circ) \approx -0.91$: same size as the value $25^\circ$ from the start, with the sign flipped.
ch15_ex6_q12c: $180^\circ$ is halfway through the cosine cycle, and that is always the minimum.
ch15_ex6_q12d: The cosine graph is symmetric about $180^\circ$, so $\cos(340^\circ) = \cos(20^\circ) \approx 0.94$.
ch15_ex6_q13b: $\cos(140^\circ) = -\cos(40^\circ) \approx -0.77$; compare with part c, which has the same size.
ch15_ex6_q13c: $\cos(40^\circ) = \sin(50^\circ) \approx 0.77$; $40^\circ$ is a bit under $45^\circ$, so the value is a bit over $0.71$.
ch15_ex6_q13d: $\cos(200^\circ) = -\cos(20^\circ) \approx -0.94$, close to the minimum of $-1$ at $180^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q14a: For cosine, the two solutions in one cycle always add to $360^\circ$: $120^\circ + 240^\circ = 360^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q14b: Link to the 3-4-5 triangle: $\cos = \frac45$ gives about $36.9^\circ$, so the reading $37^\circ$ is right.
ch15_ex6_q14c: $0.7$ is just under $\cos(45^\circ) \approx 0.707$, and cosine falls as the angle grows, so the angle is just over $45^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q15b: Once you have $26^\circ$, the other answers come free: $360^\circ - 26^\circ = 334^\circ$, then add $360^\circ$ to both.
ch15_ex6_q16: Only three numbers to learn: $0.58$, $1$ and $1.73$. Note $\tan(30^\circ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $\tan(60^\circ) = \sqrt3$ are reciprocals.
Your calculator gives an error at $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$; write 'undefined' rather than a number.
ch15_ex6_q17: Draw the dashed asymptotes first at $90^\circ, 270^\circ, 450^\circ, 630^\circ$. Each branch then passes through an $x$-intercept halfway between two asymptotes.
ch15_ex6_q18: Unit circle reason: $\theta$ and $\theta + 180^\circ$ lie on the same straight line through O, so the gradient, and therefore tan, is the same.
ch15_ex6_q19: Since $\tan = \frac{\sin}{\cos}$, the zeros of sine give the zeros of tan, and the zeros of cosine give the asymptotes.
ch15_ex6_q20a: $\tan(60^\circ) = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ exactly, so the graph reading can be checked against an exact value.
ch15_ex6_q20b: $135^\circ$ lies on the line $y = -x$, whose gradient is $-1$, so $\tan(135^\circ) = -1$ exactly.
ch15_ex6_q20c: Reduce: $310^\circ - 180^\circ = 130^\circ$, and $\tan(130^\circ) = -\tan(50^\circ) \approx -1.19$. Since $50^\circ > 45^\circ$, the size must be more than 1.
ch15_ex6_q20d: $\tan(220^\circ) = \tan(40^\circ)$, and $40^\circ < 45^\circ$, so the value must be a bit less than 1: about $0.84$.
ch15_ex6_q21c: $710^\circ$ is $10^\circ$ short of $720^\circ$ (an $x$-intercept), so the value is small and negative: $-\tan(10^\circ) \approx -0.18$.
ch15_ex6_q22a: $\tan(45^\circ) = 1$ because the $45^\circ$ right triangle is isosceles (opposite = adjacent). The other answers are $180^\circ$ apart.
ch15_ex6_q22b: Estimate first: $\tan(45^\circ) = 1$ and $\tan(60^\circ) \approx 1.73$, so a value of $1.5$ must come from an angle between them, such as $56^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q22c: Sign check: $158^\circ$ is in quadrant 2, where tan is negative, so it fits $y = -0.4$.
ch15_ex6_q22d: Since $2 > \sqrt3 \approx 1.73$, the reference angle is just over $60^\circ$ (about $63^\circ$). Placed in quadrant 2, that gives about $117^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q22e: Small-angle estimate: for small angles $\tan\theta$ is about $\theta$ in radians, so $\theta \approx 0.2 \times 57.3 \approx 11^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q22f: $\tan = -1$ on the line $y = -x$, which passes through $135^\circ$ and $315^\circ$ on the unit circle.
ch15_ex6_q23a: $\cos(-x) = \cos(x)$, so the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis: sketch $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$, then mirror it.
ch15_ex6_q23b: $720^\circ$ is exactly two periods: maxima at $90^\circ$ and $450^\circ$, minima at $270^\circ$ and $630^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q24a: The 2 makes the wave run twice as fast, so every key $x$-value halves: the maximum moves from $90^\circ$ to $45^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q24b: Use $\cos(-x) = \cos(x)$: the graph on $[-360^\circ, 0^\circ]$ mirrors the one on $[0^\circ, 360^\circ]$, with the minimum $(-180^\circ, -2)$ in the middle.
ch15_ex6_q25a: Recipe for $y = a\cos(nx)$ or $y = a\sin(nx)$: amplitude $= |a|$ and period $= \frac{360^\circ}{n}$.
ch15_ex6_q25b: The bigger $n$ is, the shorter the period: $n = 3$ squeezes three full waves into $360^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q25c: $\frac{x}{2}$ means $n = \frac12$, and $360^\circ \div \frac12 = 720^\circ$. A fraction in front of $x$ stretches the wave sideways.
ch15_ex6_q25d: $n = \frac14$ gives period $360^\circ \times 4 = 1440^\circ$; amplitude $\frac12$ means the wave only reaches $\pm 0.5$.
ch15_ex6_q25e: $y = -\sin(x)$ is the sine wave flipped: it starts at 0 and goes down first. It is the same as $y = \sin(x + 180^\circ)$.
ch15_ex6_q25f: $y = -\cos(2x)$ starts at its minimum $(0^\circ, -1)$ and returns to it at $180^\circ$, one period later.
ch15_ex6_q26a: Amplitude $= \frac{\text{max} - \text{min}}{2} = \frac{3 - (-3)}{2} = 3$. This formula still works when a graph is shifted up or down.
ch15_ex6_q26b: Link to the equation: a period of $180^\circ$ means $n = \frac{360^\circ}{180^\circ} = 2$, which you need for part c.
ch15_ex6_q26c: Build the equation in three steps: starts at a maximum means cos, amplitude 3 means $a = 3$, and period $180^\circ$ means $n = 2$.
ch15_ex6_q27a: $n = \frac13$ gives period $1080^\circ$, so the domain is exactly one cycle. The quarter points are $0^\circ, 270^\circ, 540^\circ, 810^\circ, 1080^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q27b: The quarter points are every $45^\circ$. Because of the minus sign, the first turning point, at $45^\circ$, is a minimum of $-3$.
ch15_ex6_q27c: The period of $720^\circ$ is twice the domain width of $360^\circ$, so you see only half a cycle: the rising part from $(-180^\circ, -3)$ to $(180^\circ, 3)$.
ch15_ex6_q27d: A period of $120^\circ$ gives three cycles in $360^\circ$. Mark quarter points every $30^\circ$, starting at the minimum $(0^\circ, -1)$.
ch15_ex6_q27e: The domain $[0^\circ, 180^\circ]$ is exactly one period: zeros at $45^\circ$ and $135^\circ$, minimum $(90^\circ, -5)$.
ch15_ex6_q27f: A period of $90^\circ$ means quarter points every $22.5^\circ$. The graph is inverted, so the first turning point, at $22.5^\circ$, is a minimum.
ch15_ex6_q28a: Adding 1 lifts every point by 1, so the range becomes $[0, 2]$. The graph just touches the $x$-axis at $180^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q28b: The range is $[-3, -1]$, so the whole graph sits below the $x$-axis and never crosses it.
ch15_ex6_q28c: The factor $\frac{\pi}{180}$ converts degrees to radians, so graph it with technology in radian mode. Then $x - 60$ shifts the cosine wave $60^\circ$ right.
ch15_ex6_q28d: The range is $3 \pm 2$, which is $[1, 5]$, so set the $y$-window to about 0 to 6. The period is $90^\circ$, so four cycles fit in $360^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q29a: The minimum occurs where $2x = 180^\circ$ or $540^\circ$, which gives $x = 90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$.
ch15_ex6_q29b: The range shifts with the graph: $[-1, 1]$ plus 2 gives $[1, 3]$.
ch15_ex6_q29c: General result: $y = a\sin(x) + c$ with $a > 0$ has maximum $c + a$ and minimum $c - a$. The centre line $y = c$ sits halfway between.
ch15_ex6_q30a: Use $\tan(180^\circ - x) = -\tan(x)$: once you know $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, the values at $150^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ are the negatives.
ch15_ex6_q30b: Because $\tan(180^\circ - x) = -\tan(x)$, the graph on $[0^\circ, 180^\circ]$ has half-turn symmetry about the point $(90^\circ, 0)$.
ch15_ex6_q30c: Try values near $90^\circ$: $\tan(89^\circ) \approx 57.3$ but $\tan(91^\circ) \approx -57.3$. The graph shoots off in opposite directions on either side.
ch15_ex6_q30d: Asymptotes are $180^\circ$ apart, at every odd multiple of $90^\circ$: $90^\circ, 270^\circ, 450^\circ, \ldots$
ch15_ex6_q30e: Tan has no maximum or minimum because its range is all real numbers, so there is no amplitude to measure.
ch15_ex6_q31a: Asymptotes are where $2x = 90^\circ, 270^\circ$ ($x = 45^\circ, 135^\circ$). Intercepts are where $2x = 0^\circ, 180^\circ, 360^\circ$ ($x = 0^\circ, 90^\circ, 180^\circ$).
ch15_ex6_q31b: Each asymptote lies exactly halfway between two neighbouring $x$-intercepts.
ch15_ex6_q31c: The period of $\tan(nx)$ is $\frac{180^\circ}{n}$; it is the distance between neighbouring asymptotes.
ch15_ex6_q32a: A quarter period is 3 hours, so the key times are $t = 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, \ldots$: zero, high, zero, low, zero.
ch15_ex6_q32b: Sine never exceeds 1, so $3\sin(\text{anything})$ is at most 3.
ch15_ex6_q32c: $30 \times 8 = 240^\circ$ is an exact angle: $\sin(240^\circ) = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, so $h = -\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$ exactly.
ch15_ex6_q33a: Maxima occur where $30t = 90^\circ$ ($t = 3$) and minima where $30t = 270^\circ$ ($t = 9$); then add 12 hours for the next cycle.
ch15_ex6_q33b: The high tide occurs when $\sin(30t^\circ) = 1$, at 3 am and 3 pm.
ch15_ex6_q33c: The low tide occurs when $\sin(30t^\circ) = -1$, at 9 am and 9 pm.
ch15_ex6_q34a: $t = 6$ gives $15 \times 6 = 90^\circ$ and $\cos(90^\circ) = 0$, so $T$ is exactly the middle value 22.
ch15_ex6_q34b: The period is $\frac{360}{15} = 24$ hours, so the quarter points are every 6 hours: 3 am (20), 9 am (22), 3 pm (24), 9 pm (22), 3 am (20).
ch15_ex6_q34c: The warmest time is when $15t = 180^\circ$, i.e. $t = 12$, which is 3 pm.
